overlap.title: Gifts to the treasure of the work: 61,000 drams of gold, or 41,000?
overlap.summary: At the end of the list of the first return, Ezra says 61,000 drams of gold, 5,000 pound of silver and 100 priests’ garments were given. Nehemiah’s copy of the register names three sets of givers whose gifts come to 41,000 drams of gold, 4,200 pound of silver and 597 priests’ garments, with fifty basons.
overlap.reasoning: Nehemiah’s three gifts of gold are 1,000, 20,000 and 20,000 drams, which is 41,000; his silver is 2,200 and 2,000 pound, which is 4,200; his garments are 530 and 67, which is 597. Ezra gives one set of figures, 61,000, 5,000 and 100, and credits them to “some of the chief of the fathers”. Whether Ezra’s figures are set beside Nehemiah’s totals or beside his line for the chief of the fathers alone (20,000 drams and 2,200 pound), they differ.
overlap.scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV figures of Ezra 2:69 are those of the Hebrew quoted, and Brenton’s Greek has the same three numbers. The Greek names the unit of gold as minas where the KJV has drams; that is noted as wording and no G is proposed on it. The conflict assumes that both passages report the same giving; Nehemiah presents his list as the register of those who came up at the first, and both passages stand at the same point of that list, but neither says in so many words that the gifts are the same. Only the KJV is quoted for Nehemiah 7:70–72, where the Hebrew verse numbers run one lower; Brenton’s Greek of Nehemiah was not compared. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

overlap.summary: The calendar distinguishes an evening boundary from a daytime date, and seven days in booths from an eighth-day assembly.
overlap.reasoning: The surrounding instructions explain why the ninth evening and tenth day, or seven festival days and an eighth assembly, need not be competing totals.
overlap.scope: This reading addresses these particular dates. It does not settle ancient calendar disputes, the meaning of Sabbath in the harvest count, or correspondence with modern dates.
